questions.title: How does the court's ability to take 'judicial notice' of copyright registrations affect the standard for a Rule 12(b)(6) motion?
questions.question_body: I'm confused about the procedural aspect of the ruling. The court mentions it can take 'judicial notice' of copyright registrations while reviewing the complaint for a 12(b)(6) motion. Usually, I thought a 12(b)(6) motion is strictly limited to the facts alleged in the complaint. Does this mean the court can look at external government records to decide if a claim is legally sufficient to proceed?

questions.title: How does the court distinguish between 'subjective intent' and 'objective purpose' in determining transformative use?
questions.question_body: In the fair use analysis, Santos argued that his intent in making the videos was the same as Kimmel's (to get money for absurd things). However, the court rejected this, citing the Warhol case. Can someone explain the legal distinction here? If the creator of the original work intended something specific, why does the 'reasonable observer's' interpretation trump the creator's own subjective intent in a fair use analysis?

questions.title: Why does a parody or mocking segment not count as a 'competing substitute' under the fourth fair use factor?
questions.question_body: The court states that it doesn't matter if the second work 'devalues' the first through parody, but only if it 'usurps the market.' If Kimmel’s segment makes Santos’s videos look ridiculous, isn't that a form of market harm? I'm struggling to understand why the court thinks a critical review or lampoon is automatically excluded from the 'potential licensing market' for the original work.

questions.title: What is the legal threshold for a non-party to be considered a 'third-party beneficiary' of a Terms of Service agreement?
questions.question_body: The court dismissed Santos’s breach of contract claim because he wasn't a party to the Cameo Terms of Service. It mentions a 'strong presumption against conferring benefits to noncontracting third parties' and says there must be an 'express declaration.' Does this mean that unless a contract specifically names a class of people (like 'users' or 'creators') as beneficiaries, it is almost impossible for a third party to sue over a breach of that contract?

questions.title: What constitutes 'essential terms' of a contract when pleading an implied-in-fact contract?
questions.question_body: The court dismissed the implied contract claim because Santos failed to allege the 'essential terms.' Since an implied contract isn't written down, how is a plaintiff supposed to know what the 'essential terms' are for the purpose of a complaint? Is there a standard list of elements (like price, duration, etc.) that must be pleaded to survive a 12(b)(6) motion in New York?

questions.title: Does the 'out-of-pocket loss' requirement for fraudulent inducement bar claims based purely on reputational harm?
questions.question_body: The court affirmed the dismissal of the fraudulent inducement claim because Santos didn't allege an 'out-of-pocket loss.' Under New York law, if a defendant tricks a plaintiff into doing something that ruins their reputation or causes emotional distress, but doesn't cost them actual cash, is there no way to bring a fraud claim? I'm trying to understand the scope of 'actual' loss in this context.
